title: When Prophecy Fails
text:
In 1954, a woman near Chicago, called Marian Keech in the published study (her real name was Dorothy Martin), announced that she had received messages from beings on another planet. They warned that a great flood would destroy much of North America before dawn on December 21, and that true believers would be rescued by a flying saucer. A small group gathered around her. Some quit their jobs, gave away possessions or broke with family.

Leon Festinger, Henry Riecken and Stanley Schachter, then at the University of Minnesota, saw a chance to test an idea. They predicted that if believers were deeply committed and had social support, a failed prophecy would not end their faith but would push them to seek new converts. They and their assistants joined the group, posing as believers.

On the night of December 20, the members waited at Keech's house for the saucer. Midnight passed, and nothing happened. In the early morning, Keech announced a new message: the group's faith had spread so much light that the world had been spared. The group, which had previously avoided publicity, began calling newspapers and seeking to spread its message. Believers who had waited alone, away from the others, were more likely to lose faith.
lesson: A committed group facing evidence that it was wrong may double down rather than reconsider. Build habits of admitting error before your team's identity depends on being right.
people: Leon Festinger, Henry Riecken, Stanley Schachter
source: Festinger, L., Riecken, H. W., and Schachter, S. (1956). When Prophecy Fails. University of Minnesota Press.
caveat: Later archival research has suggested that the observers influenced the group more than the book admits and that some members had sought publicity before the prophecy failed.
